claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model?, run a realistic no-rollback sequential editing benchmark on public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE using GPT-2-XL and GPT-J with ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained fine-tuning, and an unedited baseline. Filter out unrecallable/trivial facts, then apply 1, 10, 100, and 1000 cumulative edits without resetting weights. After each tranche, measure Reliability on edited prompts, Generalization on paraphrases/equivalent neighborhoods, COUNTERFACT ES/PS/NS, and retention of earlier edits. Also include canonical single-edit rollback evaluation to reproduce prior near-perfect settings. If parameter editors remain high on Reliability and Generalization across large cumulative edit counts, the main unreliability claim weakens; if scores collapse or earlier edits are overwritten while rollback results look strong, this supports the claim that prior measurements overstate reliability. This experiment could be made unnecessary by public, independently replicated no-rollback logs for the same editors, backbones, datasets, and edit counts.

To address subclaim Does parameter-based knowledge editing damage a large language model’s core capabilities?, evaluate the same edited checkpoints from the first experiment on unrelated public robustness datasets such as HellaSwag, LAMBADA, Natural Questions, and MMLU, plus perplexity on WikiText-103 or C4 validation samples. Measure pre/post accuracy, perplexity, fluency, consistency, mean-rank on held-out facts, and out-of-scope locality agreement. Include controls for generic fine-tuning, random same-norm weight perturbations, and parameter-free in-context editing where the base weights are unchanged. If edited models preserve unrelated-task performance while changing only targeted facts, the damage subclaim is weakened; if performance, calibration, perplexity, or locality degrade increasingly with edit count, this supports broad capability damage rather than harmless targeted updating. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released edited checkpoints with comprehensive unrelated-task evaluations before and after editing.

To address subclaim Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?, reproduce reported ROME, MEMIT, and MEND results on COUNTERFACT and ZSRE under the original metrics, then re-evaluate the identical edits using stricter conditions: paraphrase neighborhoods not used by the editor, subject-replacement and reversed-relation portability tests, MQuAKE multi-hop propagation, human or automated prompt validation, unrecallable-instance filtering, and sequential no-rollback evaluation. Compare original ES/PS/NS-style aggregate scores against the stricter Reliability, Generalization, Locality, and Portability breakdowns. If near-perfect scores persist across these harder probes, the prior-work critique is weakened; if high original scores coexist with poor paraphrase, portability, multi-hop, or sequential behavior, then the apparent success is an artifact of unrealistic evaluation. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a benchmark paper that already re-runs these exact editors under validated paraphrase, portability, multi-hop, and cumulative-edit protocols.

To address subclaim Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model’s representation space?, estimate layerwise representation covariance matrices from a large public text sample such as C4 or WikiText-103 for the same backbone models, compute eigenvectors/eigenvalues, and project each editor-induced activation change and weight-update-induced representation change into the eigenspace. For each edit, measure whether components lying in low-variance eigendirections produce larger downstream logit changes, larger KL divergence on unrelated prompts, or larger locality failures than components in high-variance directions. Include same-norm random perturbations and edits constrained to high-variance versus low-variance subspaces as controls. If low-variance projections systematically predict amplified output changes and damage after controlling for update norm, layer, and edit success, this supports the geometric mechanism; if amplification is unrelated to representation variance, the geometric subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released eigenspace-projection analyses connecting edit deltas, covariance spectra, and downstream damage across multiple models.

To address subclaim Do localized weight edits propagate globally?, after applying single and batched ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and fine-tuning edits, measure activation drift, attention-pattern drift, MLP-output drift, and output-distribution KL divergence across layers for three prompt sets: edited facts, semantically neighboring facts, and unrelated prompts from Natural Questions or WikiText-103. Use causal tracing and representation zeroing as parallel localization procedures, and perform layer/token sweeps to see whether a nominally local edit induces changes far from the edited layer, token, relation, or subject. If changes remain confined to the edited relation and layer while unrelated prompts are stable, the global-propagation subclaim is weakened; if small local weight deltas cause widespread layerwise activation and output-distribution shifts, especially on unrelated prompts, the subclaim is supported. This experiment could be made unnecessary by open pre/post activation caches demonstrating whether edit effects remain local or diffuse globally.

To address subclaim Is a parameter-free approach a serious alternative to parameter editing?, compare parameter-modifying editors such as ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and constrained fine-tuning against parameter-free or parameter-preserving methods such as IKE-style in-context editing, SERAC-style retrieval/memory editing, T-Patcher-style external modules, or MeLLo-style retrieval-based correction on COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, and MQuAKE. Verify that base model weights are byte-identical before and after the parameter-free method, and report Reliability, Generalization, Locality, Portability, robustness-task performance, latency, memory footprint, and cost per edit over 1 to 1000 edits. If parameter-free methods match or exceed parameter editors on edit success and robustness while preserving core-task scores and base weights, they are a serious alternative rather than a fallback; if they work only when prompts reveal the answer, fail portability, or impose prohibitive retrieval/latency costs, the alternative claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by transparent head-to-head public leaderboards that include weight hashes, resource use, and the same realistic evaluation suite for both parameter-free and parameter-editing methods.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

Its cumulative no-rollback evaluation also uses ordinary post-edit generation rather than relying only on the prior rollback setup, so the team would learn whether the apparent single-edit success survives an honest inference protocol.

reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set varies two backbones, several editor families, multiple factual tasks, and filters out unrecallable or trivial instances; it also uses perturbation and subspace controls. It does not test substantially larger models, event-level knowledge, explicit high- versus low-confidence fact strata, or systematic hyperparameter/architecture sensitivity of the strongest surviving editor. Consequently it addresses some incidental explanations but leaves major scope explanations open.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment rules out several alternative explanations by varying scale, knowledge representation, fact difficulty, and the configuration of the least-collapsing method.
[2] The proposed set varies backbones and methods and removes some trivial or unrecallable facts, so it provides limited robustness evidence.
[3] It does not include a larger-scale sweep, event-level facts, confidence-stratified facts, or a dedicated sensitivity analysis of a robust editor.
[4] Therefore a collapse observed in the proposed set could still be specific to the selected model scale, fact representation, difficulty filtering, or editor configuration.
[5] A team running the proposed set would fail to learn whether the limitation persists across those omitted scales, knowledge types, fact strata, and configurations.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed union directly tests realistic cumulative reliability, collateral capability damage, global propagation, the low-variance geometric hypothesis, and whether a parameter-preserving method leaves weights unchanged while competing on editing and resource measures. It would therefore make the central claim testable within the selected models and benchmarks. It would not fully settle the claim at the strength of the reference study because the scoring-instrument validation lacks an explicit deterministic token-level cross-check, the geometric analysis does not explicitly establish monotonic normalized low-variance amplification across cumulative counts, and generality across scale, event-level knowledge, fact strata, and editor configurations remains incomplete.
missing: An explicit deterministic token-level match-ratio/exact-match validation against the semantic editing scores.
